scams.name: St. Louis 'Purple Shirt' Intersection Window-Approach Scam
scams.description:
Travelers have tracked the same individuals working the same corners for years, operating under "Saving the Lost" or similar unregistered religious framing. The most recent reports describe men aggressively soliciting donations in traffic, and earlier accounts document the same men working the same corners.

The approach is aggressive and theatrical. A man in a branded purple shirt stands at the median of a red-light intersection and yells to drivers to roll down their windows. The opening line is religious — "Brother, have you accepted Jesus?" or "Sister, I need prayers" — and pivots within ten seconds to a demand for cash, gift cards, or a donation through a tap-to-pay card reader.

The branded-shirt framing is the hook. The shirts carry logos for "Saving the Lost Ministries" or similar names, which travelers have researched and found to be unregistered organizations. Community investigations into the men in the purple "Saving the Lost" shirts turned up no IRS 501(c)(3) filings.

The volume is significant. The same individuals work the same corners daily for years, treating the scam as a steady income. Drivers who make a U-turn to avoid the intersection or refuse eye contact are often followed on foot for a short distance, with the yelling continuing.

To defend yourself, do not roll down your car window at St. Louis intersections when a stranger approaches. Keep your windows up, your eyes forward, and your hands on the wheel. If the stranger follows on foot, drive away at the first safe opportunity. Do not engage with any religious or charity pitch delivered through a car window at a red light.

If you are followed aggressively or blocked from moving, call 911 for an immediate response. For formal complaints, the St. Louis Metropolitan Police non-emergency line is 314-231-1212. Report the pattern to the Missouri Attorney General Consumer Protection Division at 800-392-8222 and to the FTC at reportfraud.ftc.gov. To verify the tax-exempt status of any "ministry" claiming 501(c)(3), check the IRS Tax Exempt Organization Search at IRS.gov.
scams.avoidance: Keep your car windows up and your eyes forward at St. Louis red lights when a stranger approaches the vehicle. Never tap a handheld card reader through a car window for any reason or cause. Make a U-turn at the light or take an alternate route if the intersection is known for aggressive approach patterns. Verify any "ministry" or "charity" 501(c)(3) status at the IRS Tax Exempt Organization Search on IRS.gov before donating. If you are blocked or followed aggressively, call 911 or the St. Louis Metropolitan Police non-emergency line at 314-231-1212.
scams.location: Hanley Road and I-64 exit ramp, Brentwood Boulevard intersections, Page Avenue and Woodson Road, Central West End and Forest Park perimeter, Clayton commercial corridor, downtown St. Louis pedestrian intersections
scams.tldr: St. Louis has a locally famous intersection scam: men in branded purple shirts yell at drivers stopped at red lights to roll their windows down.

scams.name: STL Airport Fake Uber & Rideshare Impersonation
scams.description:
Unlicensed operators intercept real Uber and Lyft riders at STL Airport arrivals, impersonate the app-assigned driver, and run unlicensed rides at inflated fares. The pattern mirrors the Seattle and Houston fake-Uber scams, and travelers have documented the exact mechanic: a driver receiving spoofed calls through the Uber app during his first-day St. Louis shift.

The St. Louis version relies on app-call spoofing. A St. Louis Uber driver reported receiving calls through the Uber app on his first-day pickup, from a caller pretending to be the rider and redirecting the driver to the wrong address. The real rider was then approached by the fake driver at the airport curb. Travelers across multiple US cities have reported similar driver-side calls.

The extra-stop variant targets riders. Fraudsters add a third destination to the trip just before the driver arrives, then cancel for a refund while the real rider waits. At STL, both drivers and riders appear to be targeted based on vehicle availability in the pickup queue.

The national pattern is well established. The Philadelphia Parking Authority's investigation into imposter rideshares shows that the same technique scales across US airports, and bonus-notification fraud adds a driver-targeting overlay specific to St. Louis markets.

To defend yourself, always verify the license plate, vehicle make, model, and driver name in the Uber or Lyft app before opening any door at STL. Do not respond to phone calls through the Uber or Lyft app unless you initiated them. Use MetroLink from STL Airport to downtown St. Louis as the scam-proof backup — $2.00 to $4.00 one-way, about 40 minutes to 8th and Pine downtown.

If you are overcharged or misled, call STL Airport Police at 314-890-1500 for airport incidents. For downtown rideshare issues, the St. Louis Metropolitan Police non-emergency line is 314-231-1212. Report the pattern to the Missouri Attorney General Consumer Protection Division at 800-392-8222, and dispute fraudulent rideshare charges with your card issuer within 48 hours.
scams.avoidance: Always verify the license plate, vehicle make, model, and driver name in the Uber or Lyft app before opening any door. Use the designated rideshare pickup zone at STL and confirm the vehicle plate matches the app before entering. Take MetroLink from STL Airport to downtown St. Louis for $2.00 to $4.00 one-way in about 40 minutes. Do not respond to inbound phone calls through the Uber or Lyft app unless you initiated the contact. Dispute fraudulent rideshare charges with your card issuer within 48 hours and report to STL Airport Police at 314-890-1500.
scams.location: St. Louis Lambert International Airport (STL) Terminal 1 and Terminal 2 arrivals, STL rideshare pickup zones, Central West End MetroLink station, downtown St. Louis hotel curbsides, Clayton commercial district pickups
scams.tldr: Fake-Uber pickups at St. Louis Lambert International Airport target arriving tourists with the same script as Seattle and Houston.

scams.name: Forest Park 'Stranded Stranger' & Intersection Panhandling
scams.description:
A woman pulls over on the side of a Forest Park road, pretends to be stranded, and waves drivers down. The mechanic is the same multi-state "out of gas" ring seen in Minneapolis and Dallas, adapted to St. Louis's Forest Park tourist corridor.

The Forest Park variant targets weekend visitors. The scammer parks at a visible turnoff inside the park, pops the hood, and waves down passing cars. When a driver stops, she explains that her card is not working, her phone is dead, and she needs gas money to get home. The jewelry-as-collateral close follows: a "gold" ring or necklace handed over as a promise of future repayment.

The intersection panhandling pattern is separate and long-running. As panhandling complaints grow, cities in St. Louis County have tweaked their laws, which provides the enforcement context. At the Brentwood and I-64 corner, the same family has worked the same spot for months.

The distinguishing signal is location consistency. The same individuals appear at the same Forest Park turnoffs and the same suburban intersections for extended periods, treating the scam as a steady income. The pattern has been documented for over a decade.

To defend yourself, never stop for a "stranded" stranger inside Forest Park or at a St. Louis suburban intersection. If the situation looks genuinely dangerous, call 911 from a safe distance to dispatch help rather than stopping yourself. Keep your car windows up and doors locked at intersections when pedestrians approach.

Never accept a ring, necklace, or watch from a stranger as collateral against a promised repayment — the items are always costume jewelry worth a dollar or less. If you have been conned, file a report with the St. Louis Metropolitan Police non-emergency line at 314-231-1212 and with the Missouri Attorney General Consumer Protection Division at 800-392-8222. For Forest Park-specific incidents, the St. Louis Park Rangers are reachable at 314-289-5300.
scams.avoidance: Never stop for a "stranded" stranger inside Forest Park or at a St. Louis suburban intersection. Keep your car windows up and doors locked at St. Louis intersections when pedestrians approach the vehicle. Never accept a gold-looking ring, necklace, or watch from a stranger as collateral under any circumstances. If the situation looks genuinely dangerous, call 911 from a safe distance to dispatch help. Report aggressive panhandling patterns to the St. Louis Metropolitan Police at 314-231-1212 or the Park Rangers at 314-289-5300.
scams.location: Forest Park interior roads and parking lots, Brentwood Boulevard and I-64 interchange, Hanley Road exit ramps, Gravois Avenue south St. Louis corridors, Downtown Loop entrance medians, Grand Boulevard intersections
scams.tldr: A woman pretends to be stranded on a Forest Park road — card not working, phone dead, needing gas money — and hands over "gold" jewelry as collateral she never intends to reclaim.

scams.name: Missouri DOR 'Traffic Violation' Text & Phone Scam
scams.description:
On April 22, 2026, FOX 2 St. Louis reported that St. Louis County Police had issued a formal public warning after a community-wide surge in complaints. Scam texts impersonate the Missouri Department of Revenue, claim an unpaid traffic violation with "FINAL NOTICE" framing, and demand immediate payment through a cloned Missouri e-filing portal.

The mechanic is classic phishing with government-branded framing. After one Missouri resident posted the exact message wording — "Scam text? Wife received this today" — the report spread widely. The link in the text resolves to a domain that visually mimics the official Missouri DOR site (dor.mo.gov) but with subtle URL differences: mo-gov-dor.com, mo-dor-pay.net, and rotating variants.

The payment flow captures card data. The cloned site walks the victim through "paying the fine" with a credit-card form that stores the numbers, CVV, and billing address for later fraud. Travelers nationally have documented the identical pattern, with Missouri being a recent focus area.

The enforcement response has scaled up. St. Louis police overtime has exploded amid a broader police-workload surge, and Northern News Now coverage in July 2025 and April 2026 confirmed ongoing St. Louis County warnings. The St. Louis County Sheriff issued public alerts about local scam calls and texts within the last week of this writing.

To defend yourself, remember that the Missouri Department of Revenue does not send traffic-violation notices by text message. All legitimate DOR communications arrive by certified US Mail with a case number, a dor.mo.gov URL, and a 573-751-xxxx phone contact. If you receive a "FINAL NOTICE" text with a pay-now link, it is always a scam — delete it without clicking.

If you clicked and entered card details, change every password on accounts that use similar credentials, dispute any new card charges with your issuer, and freeze your credit at Experian, Equifax, and TransUnion. File reports with the St. Louis County Police non-emergency line at 636-529-8210 and the Missouri Attorney General Consumer Protection Division at 800-392-8222. For national identity-theft response, file with the FTC at identitytheft.gov.
scams.avoidance: Delete without clicking any text message claiming to be from the Missouri DOR or a St. Louis County Court; legitimate notices arrive by certified mail. Verify any suspected real traffic-violation notice by calling the Missouri DOR at 573-751-3505 or visiting dor.mo.gov directly. Never enter credit-card details on a site reached via a text link, regardless of how official it appears. If you clicked and entered details, change your passwords immediately and freeze your credit at Experian, Equifax, and TransUnion. File identity-theft reports at identitytheft.gov and scam-pattern reports with the Missouri Attorney General at 800-392-8222.
scams.location: Missouri-wide SMS and phone-call targets, Statewide Missouri Department of Revenue impersonation, St. Louis County Court impersonation, Missouri State Patrol traffic citation impersonation, Missouri e-filing portals spoofed
scams.tldr: A fraudulent traffic-ticket text scam is sweeping Missouri in 2026, impersonating the state Department of Revenue.
